nature-econ-483.title: Gross domestic product: an economy in one number
nature-econ-483.text: William Petty wanted to know how heavy a tax burden England could bear during the Anglo-Dutch wars of 1652 to 1674. His answer was an early version of the most quoted number in economics. Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a set period, usually a year. Final goods are those bought by their last user, not parts that go into something else. GDP adds up four major components: spending by households, spending by government, investment in new capital, and exports minus imports. Simon Kuznets developed the modern concept for a 1934 report to the US Congress. After the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944, GDP became the main tool for measuring a country's economy, and today it is the usual way to compare countries. The international rulebook for measuring it is the 2008 edition of {{ref:nature-econ-596}}, prepared by the IMF, EU, OECD, UN and World Bank. Kuznets himself warned against using GDP to measure welfare. It is not a measure of overall living standards or well-being, since it ignores how income is shared. Critics also fault it for leaving out resource extraction, environmental damage and unpaid domestic work.

nature-econ-478.title: Economic growth and the power of small percentages
nature-econ-478.text: Over long periods, even a small growth rate such as 2% a year has large effects. Economic growth is an increase in the amount and quality of the goods and services a society produces. It is usually measured as the rise in an economy's output over a year or longer. The figure is adjusted for inflation so that rising prices do not distort the picture. The rate is typically calculated from inflation-adjusted GDP, either in total or per person, or from measures such as national income per person or median income. Adam Smith pioneered modern growth theory in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. He named two main drivers: the division of labour and the accumulation of capital. Historically, the most important source of real growth per person has been rising output per unit of labour. Growth has a shadow, though. So far, economic growth and carbon dioxide emissions have been closely correlated across nations, although the carbon emitted per unit of GDP varies widely. Worries about this harm have led some to argue for slower growth, or for abandoning growth altogether.

nature-econ-541.title: Macroeconomics: studying the economy as a whole
nature-econ-541.text: When Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936, he gave economics a new branch. Macroeconomics studies how a whole economy, regional, national or global, performs and behaves. It differs from microeconomics, which studies smaller units such as single firms, consumers and markets. Macroeconomists study economy-wide totals: GDP, national income, unemployment, inflation, consumption, saving, investment and trade. Three variables sit at the center: output, unemployment and inflation. The topics divide by time frame. The short term brings the swings of the business cycle, the alternating booms and slumps. The medium term concerns the levels of variables such as unemployment, and the long term concerns growth. The field also analyses how governments and central banks manage money and public budgets, especially when they aim to stabilize the economy or its growth rate. One accounting fact underlies it all: everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, and total net output is usually measured as GDP. Since World War II, Keynesians, monetarists, new classical and new Keynesian economists have shaped mainstream research.

nature-econ-566.title: National accounts: double-entry books for a whole country
nature-econ-566.text: Colin Clark and Simon Kuznets made the first efforts in the late 1920s and 1930s, spurred by the Great Depression and the needs of Keynesian policy. What they began became national accounts: a complete and consistent set of accounts for measuring a nation's economic activity, built on double-entry bookkeeping. Double entry makes both sides of an account equal even though they measure different things, such as production and the income it generates. The accounts record the output, spending and income of households, corporations and government, their links with other countries, and their net worth. They present both flows over a period and stocks at its end, and reconcile the two. GDP, perhaps the most widely cited measure of economic activity, is one of their totals. Figures can be nominal, at the prices of the time, or real, with the effect of price changes removed. Growth rates are usually measured in real terms. National statistical offices or central banks compile the accounts, yearly and quarterly, from surveys, censuses and administrative data. The United States published the first formal national accounts in 1947, and the UN published its first international guide to them in 1952.

nature-econ-522.title: Fiscal policy: steering the economy with taxes and spending
nature-econ-522.text: Fiscal policy grew out of the Great Depression of the 1930s, when the earlier hands-off approach to managing the economy stopped working. It is a government's use of taxes and spending to influence the economy. It rests on Keynes's theory that changing taxes and government spending shifts aggregate demand, the total spending in an economy, and with it economic activity. Governments use it to steady the economy through the business cycle. Fiscal policy usually runs through a government department. Its partner, {{ref:nature-econ-560}}, handles the amount of money and interest rates, usually through a central bank. Spending can be paid for by taxes, by printing money, called seigniorage, or by borrowing at home or abroad. A deficit is often funded by issuing bonds, and if revenue cannot cover the interest, a nation may default. Developing countries collect about half as much tax as a share of GDP as developed countries, which limits their fiscal policy.

nature-econ-596.title: The System of National Accounts: one rulebook for the world
nature-econ-596.text: Almost every country keeps its national accounts by the same rulebook. The System of National Accounts, called the United Nations System of National Accounts until 1993, is the international standard set of concepts and methods for compiling them. More than 200 countries, territories and areas have adopted it, often with local adaptations. Using it is voluntary, but following it improves data quality and makes figures comparable between countries and over time. The roots are old. William Petty made the first known attempt in England in 1665, aiming to estimate national income and wealth. A global standard was first proposed at the League of Nations in 1928, but World War 2 interrupted the work. The UN published the first standard in 1953, with revisions in 1960, 1964, 1968, 1993 and 2008, and SNA 2025 is due to be published in 2026. Its most common criticism is that its concepts and classifications do not adequately reflect real-world activities and relationships.

nature-econ-583.title: Purchasing power parity: comparing what money can buy
nature-econ-583.text: A computer costs 500 US dollars in New York and 2000 HK dollars in Hong Kong. If the same thing should cost the same everywhere, that implies 4 HK dollars per US dollar. This is purchasing power parity, or PPP. It compares currencies by what the same basket of goods costs in each country, giving an exchange rate based on purchasing power. It applies the law of one price to whole baskets. Economists use PPP to compare countries' GDP, output per worker, consumption and cost of living. The OECD's basket covers around 3,000 consumer goods and services, 30 government occupations, 200 types of equipment and about 15 construction projects. PPP suits comparisons of whole economies, where goods that are never traded matter, while market exchange rates suit single traded goods. The calculations are disputed, because comparable baskets are hard to find and people in different countries buy different things. The global poverty line is converted between currencies with PPP rates, though high-end goods that poor people rarely buy skew them.

nature-econ-487.title: GDP per capita: the average slice of the pie
nature-econ-487.text: Divide a country's GDP by its population and you get GDP per capita, its average production per person. Its great advantage as a gauge of living standards is practical: it is measured frequently, widely and consistently across countries. Adjusted for purchasing power parity, it helps compare living standards between nations. Its weakness lies in the word average. Like total GDP, it ignores how income is distributed, and it tends to overstate the income of a typical person. In some countries, growth in median income, the income of the person in the middle, has diverged from growth in GDP per capita.

nature-econ-486.title: Nominal and real GDP: stripping out inflation
nature-econ-486.text: Suppose GDP rises from $100 million to $300 million while inflation halves the value of money. On paper the economy has tripled. In fact real GDP grew 50 percent, not 200 percent. Nominal GDP is measured at the current market prices of the time, so it does not account for inflation. Real GDP adjusts for changes in the value of money so that years can be compared. The factor that converts GDP from current to constant values is called the {{ref:nature-econ-526}}. Real GDP is the basis of the GDP growth rate, usually expressed as a percentage change from the previous year.

nature-econ-480.title: Can growth and a healthy planet coexist?
nature-econ-480.text: In 2019, 11,000 scientists signed a warning that named economic growth as the driving force behind the overuse of ecosystems. Can an economy keep growing without wrecking the natural systems it rests on? The sources do not agree. Critics such as those in {{ref:nature-hist-026}} argue that a narrow focus on growth, together with globalization, risks a systemic collapse of the resources nature provides. A 2019 Global Assessment by {{ref:nature-gov-020}} warned that, given heavy losses of biodiversity, society should not focus solely on economic growth. A 2021 review for the British Treasury by {{ref:nature-hist-046}} argued that human demands far exceed nature's capacity, and called for abandoning GDP as the measure of success. Academics have proposed responses from eco-taxes and green investment to the ideas in {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}, {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}. Optimists see it differently. Julian Simon argued in 1981 that the large-scale ecological effects of growth are minor, and that human ingenuity would adapt to any that exist. Growth-oriented environmental economists instead propose government action to shift energy production toward wind, solar, hydroelectric and nuclear power. Whether growth's ecological effects are minor and manageable or are driving ecosystems toward collapse remains disputed.

nature-econ-479.title: Where growth comes from
nature-econ-479.text: Robert Solow estimated that technological progress accounted for 80 percent of the long-term rise in US income per person, and more capital investment for only 20 percent. Output per person can be broken into four parts. They are output per hour of labour, hours worked, the share of working-age people in work, and the share of people who are of working age. Capital helps, but only up to a point. More capital per worker raises output, yet it faces diminishing returns, partly because of the growing burden of depreciation. Many analyses give a major role to human capital, though it is hard to measure because it is built at home, at school and on the job. It helps growth only if the population is healthy and well nourished. History adds other forces. Moving workers from low-productivity farming to high-productivity manufacturing raised overall output, and laws protecting contracts and private property helped economies move toward capitalism.

nature-econ-552.title: Putting nature into models of the whole economy
nature-econ-552.text: In 1865, Jevons's book The Coal Question made an unsettling argument: in a growing economy, productivity gains could speed up resource scarcity. Economists have since tried to build nature into macroeconomic models, especially growth models, by adding resource scarcity and {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. During the oil crises of the 1970s, Stiglitz and Solow added resources that run out to growth models, asking whether living standards could keep rising. The 2006 {{ref:nature-clim-268}} gave the first comprehensive analysis of global economic damage from projected climate change. Integrated assessment models, pioneered by {{ref:nature-hist-050}} and covered in {{ref:nature-clim-248}}, are now widely used to estimate regional and global climate damages under different policies. Such models treat land, water and energy as inputs to production. Early work by {{ref:nature-hist-040}} replaced the familiar picture of money circling between households and firms with one driven by solar energy. How to count environmental goods and services in national accounts is still debated.

nature-econ-542.title: Inflation and deflation: when all prices move together
nature-econ-542.text: Inflation is a general rise in prices across a whole economy, and deflation is a general fall. Economists track both with price indexes. Inflation tends to rise when an economy overheats and grows too fast, while a shrinking economy can push it down or into deflation. Shocks to supply also move it, as in the oil crises of the 1970s and the 2021–2023 global energy crisis. High inflation and deflation both raise uncertainty, especially when they come unexpectedly. That is why most central banks aim for low, stable, positive inflation. An old idea, the quantity theory of money, says prices change because the amount of money changes. It has proved unreliable over short and medium horizons.

nature-econ-586.title: Real GDP: measuring output, not prices
nature-econ-586.text: Because of inflation, nominal GDP can rise even when an economy makes exactly the same physical output. Real GDP removes that illusion. It values output with the effect of price changes taken out, so it tracks the quantity produced. The method is to value every year's quantities at the prices of one base year, so that differences reflect only changes in volume. Dividing nominal GDP by real GDP gives the {{ref:nature-econ-526}}, which equals 100 in the base year and shows overall price change. Annual real GDP growth is nominal growth adjusted for inflation, usually given as a percentage. Real GDP is also called constant GDP, and organizations use different base years, such as UNCTAD's 2015 constant prices. It is one case of the general distinction between real and nominal values.

nature-econ-543.title: Unemployment: who counts as out of work
nature-econ-543.text: Not everyone without a job is unemployed. Retired people, students and discouraged job-seekers are outside the labour force, the people working or seeking work, so they are not counted. Unemployment covers people in the labour force who have no job but are actively looking for one, and the unemployment rate gives them as a percentage. Part of it is cyclical, rising and falling with the business cycle. Part is a lasting structural, or natural, level. Search, or frictional, unemployment arises because matching workers to vacancies takes time when information is imperfect. Minimum wages, trade unions and efficiency wages, pay set above the going rate to motivate staff, can hold wages above the level where supply equals demand. Okun's law ties unemployment to short-run GDP growth: in its original version, a 3% rise in output cuts unemployment by 1%.

nature-econ-569.title: Green national accounting: putting a value on nature
nature-econ-569.text: Ordinary measures of national wealth usually leave environmental assets out, partly because they are hard to value. In effect, they count them as worth zero. Green national accounting is the proposed alternative: a method of putting values on those assets. It also aims to show whether welfare can be sustained while the environment is being degraded. The methods are not settled. How to include environmental goods and services in national output is still under discussion.

nature-econ-597.title: Greening the national accounts: a half-century effort
nature-econ-597.text: For decades, the world's standard rulebook for national accounts left out the natural world that holds the economy up. Critics argued that the System of National Accounts ignored the environment that contains and supports the economy. It did not value resource stocks, their running down, or ecosystem services. Leaving out pollution costs meant the accounts overstated the net benefits of economic activity. Change came slowly. SNA 1993 first introduced environmental side accounts linked to the main ones, described in {{ref:nature-econ-598}}. It also introduced a net domestic product adjusted for resources used up, though not formally within the framework. The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, or SEEA, followed the {{ref:nature-hist-003}} in Rio in 1992, and its Central Framework became a UN standard in February 2012. SNA 2025 goes further. It formally recognizes natural capital and ecosystem services and treats the using up of resources as a cost of production. In early 2025 at least 94 countries had produced at least one SEEA account in the past five years, 67 of them regularly. The argument is not over. Environmentalists say the SNA still undervalues nature, while statisticians note that measurement methods remain unsettled.
